Асахи Шимбун

15 ноября 2026 в 07:00 JST

Временное хранилище отработавшего ядерного топлива, построенное в Муцу, префектура Аомори, является первым в стране, построенным за пределами атомных электростанций. (Фото файла Ашахи Шимбуна)

МУТСУ, префектура Аомори — Знакомое лицо может помешать третьему требованию Kansai Electric Power Co. использовать здесь временное хранилище для сокращения растущих запасов отработанного ядерного топлива.

Это третья попытка Kansai Electric получить доступ к складу, и до сих пор другие стороны, похоже, готовы одобрить этот шаг.

Объект, завершенный в конце 2024 года, был построен для хранения отработанного топлива только от Tokyo Electric Power Co. и Japan Atomic Power Co.

Тем не менее, две компании в сентябре объявили о планах получить одобрение от префектуры Аомори и муниципальных органов власти Муцу для Kansai Electric и Tohoku Electric Power Co. также использовать хранилище.

TEPCO и Japan Atomic Power заявили, что их собственные грузы не будут заполнять ожидаемую мощность объекта.

Конструкция вместе с другим зданием, которое будет построено позже, будет иметь мощность 5000 тонн, хранящихся в течение максимум 50 лет.

TEPCO и Japan Atomic Power планируют отправить на место 3500 тонн и 900 тонн соответственно. Оставшиеся 600 тонн мощности планируется направить в компании Kansai Electric (500 тонн) и Tohoku Electric (100 тонн).

Больше энергии, больше налогового восстановления

Kansai Electric впервые объяснила план местным жителям на открытых брифингах, состоявшихся в Муцу 31 октября и 1 ноября. В мероприятии приняли участие представители Kansai Electric, Tohoku Electric, TEPCO, Japan Atomic Power и правительства города Муцу.

Ожидается, что представители Муцу будут приветствовать это предложение.

Муниципальная ассамблея Муцу в марте приняла петицию, представленную местными лидерами бизнеса, которая призвала больше компаний использовать сайт.

Поскольку город вводит налоги на хранение отработанного топлива, работа ниже мощности приведет к более низким доходам, чем ожидалось.

В августе мэр Муцу Томоя Ямамото призвал TEPCO и другие заинтересованные стороны расширить использование объекта для дополнительных электроэнергетических компаний.

Согласно предложению, Kansai Electric и Tohoku Electric начнут перекачивать отработанное топливо примерно в 2028 году. Ожидается, что хранилище достигнет своей полной мощности к первой половине 2050-х годов.

Однако первоначальное соглашение о размещении на объекте не предусматривает хранения отработанного топлива от компаний, отличных от TEPCO и Japan Atomic Power.

Для изменения соглашения потребуется поддержка со стороны префектуры.

Президент TEPCO Томоаки Кобаякава заявил, что предлагаемая договоренность никоим образом не будет создавать неудобств для местных чиновников и жителей.

«Мы не считаем, что это повлияет на безопасность объекта», — сказал Кобаякава, когда он посетил городское правительство 18 сентября, чтобы объяснить изменение плана.

Он также пообещал, что новые партнеры по проекту будут соблюдать 50-летний лимит хранения.

Привязан к ядерной круговой политике

Временное хранилище отработанного топлива Mutsu, первое в Японии, построенное за пределами атомных электростанций, является важной частью политики ядерного топливного цикла страны.

Атомные электростанции в Японии эксплуатируются под предлогом повторного использования плутония и урана, извлеченных из отработанного топлива, произведенного по всей стране.

Отработанное топливо должно быть доставлено на строящийся завод по переработке ядерного топлива в Роккашо, деревне также в префектуре Аомори, в соответствии с политикой ядерного топливного цикла.

Завершение работы перерабатывающей установки, однако, было отложено в 27 раз по сравнению с первоначальной целью 1997 года из-за ряда проблем, включая длительные проверки безопасности со стороны Управления по ядерному регулированию.

Последняя дата завершения была в текущем финансовом году. Но этого вряд ли удастся достичь.

Почти трехлетняя задержка сильно ударила по электроэнергетическим компаниям, в частности, по Kansai Electric.

До Великого землетрясения в Восточной Японии в 2011 году на долю атомной энергетики компании приходилось более 50 процентов от общего объема производства электроэнергии, что делает ее самой зависимой от ядерной энергии среди всех коммунальных предприятий.

В настоящее время в нем эксплуатируется семь реакторов, что также больше, чем в любой другой полезной области.

Бежать из пространства

Запасы отработанного топлива Kansai Electric в его бассейнах близки к мощности. Ожидается, что бассейны будут заполнены с 2028 финансового года, а это означает, что атомные электростанции компании будут вынуждены выйти из строя, если они не найдут место для передачи переполненного отработанного топлива.

Компания управляет всеми своими атомными станциями в префектуре Фукуи и стремится сократить объем отработанного топлива, перемещая часть отходов за пределы префектуры.

Будет ли предоставлен доступ к хранилище Mutsu, является насущной проблемой для коммунальных служб.

Поскольку дата запуска завода по переработке в Роккашо остается неопределенной, Kansai Electric ранее стремилась использовать временное хранилище Mutsu.

Но тогда мэр Муцу Соитиро Мияшита, который сейчас является губернатором Аомори, дважды отрицал этот шаг.

В 2018 году Миясита выступила категорически против плана, когда новостные агентства сообщили, что Kansai Electric рассматривает возможность использования хранилища до того, как компания проинформировала местных чиновников или жителей.

«Мы ничего не слышали от Kansai Electric», — сказал он. «Решение компанией этого вопроса показало неуважение к чувствам местных жителей».

В 2020 году Федерация электроэнергетических компаний Японии (FEPC), отраслевое лобби, взяла на себя инициативу по обеспечению одобрения совместного использования места хранения компаниями-членами в явной попытке помочь Kansai Electric.

Мияшита снова отклонил этот шаг, сославшись на проблему с изображением Муцу.

«Если Муцу начнет принимать отработанное ядерное топливо со всей страны, город будет восприниматься как свалка для ядерных материалов», — сказал он.

Инсайдеры отрасли заявили, что Tohoku Electric была доставлена на борт на этот раз, чтобы отвлечь внимание от Kansai Electric.

Нозому Мори, президент Kansai Electric, который также является председателем FEPC, отметил на очередной пресс-конференции FEPC 18 сентября, что его компания столкнулась с постоянными проблемами в отношении проблемы отработанного топлива.

Но, добавил он, предложение о расширении использования объекта Муцу призвано расширить возможности для всей отрасли.

Kansai Electric также использовала другие варианты, включая строительство временного хранилища в Каминосеки, городе в префектуре Ямагути, для совместного использования с Chugoku Electric Power Co.

Этот план был объявлен три года назад, но компания столкнулась с яростным противодействием со стороны жителей Каминосеки и чиновников, и никаких дополнительных подробностей о проекте не было предоставлено.

Некоторые представители Kansai Electric признали, что их компания в последние месяцы смягчила разговоры о проекте Каминосеки.

Последует ли новая попытка Kansai Electric в Муцу, по-видимому, в руках Мияшиты.

Miyashita уже отклонила использование TEPCO временного хранилища Mutsu в текущем финансовом году из-за неопределенности в отношении завода по переработке в Роккашо.

Многие наблюдатели говорят, что электроэнергетика и центральное правительство должны представить реалистичный взгляд на то, когда завод будет готов к работе, если они хотят, чтобы правительство рассматривало совместное использование хранилища Mutsu.

(Эта статья была написана Томоки Моришита, Арата Мицуи, Кунихико Ода и Рюхей Цутсуи.)

Серия, основанная на дипломатических документах, рассекреченных МИД Японии

Здесь собрана информация из первых рук о выживших после атомной бомбардировки «хибакуша».

Специалисты по кулинарии, повара и другие специалисты, занимающиеся пищевыми продуктами, представляют свои особые рецепты, переплетенные с их жизненными путями.

articles.originalTitle: As inflation rises, more bereaved children seek scholarships
articles.originalText: The Ashinaga Foundation, a Tokyo-based group that supports children who have lost parents, will award scholarships to a record-high 2,196 high school students in fiscal 2026. The organization, founded in 1993, said rising living costs have deepened financial hardships among bereaved families, leading more students to seek assistance. “I was deeply shocked to learn that commodity price hikes are limiting educational opportunities for children,” Osamu Murata, president of the Ashinaga Foundation, said at a news conference on Sept. 17.
articles.originalFullText:
By YUKIHITO TAKAHAMA/ Staff Writer

November 15, 2026 at 07:00 JST

Osamu Murata, second from right, president of the Ashinaga Foundation, speaks at a news conference on Sept. 17 in Tokyo’s Chiyoda Ward. (Yukihito Takahama)

The Ashinaga Foundation, a Tokyo-based group that supports children who have lost parents, will award scholarships to a record-high 2,196 high school students in fiscal 2026.

The organization, founded in 1993, said rising living costs have deepened financial hardships among bereaved families, leading more students to seek assistance.

“I was deeply shocked to learn that commodity price hikes are limiting educational opportunities for children,” Osamu Murata, president of the Ashinaga Foundation, said at a news conference on Sept. 17.

Recipients will receive 30,000 yen ($190) per month and be exempted from repayment obligations under the foundation’s scholarship program for high school students.

The Ashinaga Foundation solicits applications each fiscal year.

Up to 3,448 high school students applied in fiscal 2026, the second-highest number on record after fiscal 2024.

Taking into account its donation-funded budget, the Ashinaga Foundation approved new grants for 2,196 students, or 63.7 percent of the applicants.

A total of 4,946 high school students are currently receiving Ashinaga scholarships.

The Ashinaga Foundation conducted a survey in August this year, covering 4,590 guardians of children receiving grants under the scholarship program. It received responses from 59.6 percent of them.

The survey found that 91.6 percent of respondents had reduced spending on food, while 15.7 percent acknowledged they had been unable to pay their rent at least once during the past year.

Respondents reported an average annual income of 1.781 million yen, little changed from 1.764 million yen in the comparable 2021 survey.

Asked about the impact of rising prices on education, 21.5 percent said they had already “given up on attending a university, college or vocational school, or feared they might have to.”

The Ashinaga Foundation plans to provide financial aid to more recipients by raising awareness of its program and strengthening fundraising efforts.

NEW AID FOR 6TH-GRADERS

The Ashinaga Foundation on Sept. 17 also announced plans to start a program offering one-time grants to sixth-grade elementary school students to help them prepare for junior high school.

The foundation will provide 50,000 yen each to 400 elementary school students to help cover rising costs for school uniforms and educational materials.

The Ashinaga Foundation hopes the one-off payment will serve as an entry point to ongoing support, including the provision of information on other assistance programs.

Osamu Murata, second from right, president of the Ashinaga Foundation, speaks at a news conference on Sept. 17 in Tokyo’s Chiyoda Ward. (Yukihito Takahama)

The Ashinaga Foundation, a Tokyo-based group that supports children who have lost parents, will award scholarships to a record-high 2,196 high school students in fiscal 2026.

The organization, founded in 1993, said rising living costs have deepened financial hardships among bereaved families, leading more students to seek assistance.

“I was deeply shocked to learn that commodity price hikes are limiting educational opportunities for children,” Osamu Murata, president of the Ashinaga Foundation, said at a news conference on Sept. 17.

Recipients will receive 30,000 yen ($190) per month and be exempted from repayment obligations under the foundation’s scholarship program for high school students.

The Ashinaga Foundation solicits applications each fiscal year.

Up to 3,448 high school students applied in fiscal 2026, the second-highest number on record after fiscal 2024.

Taking into account its donation-funded budget, the Ashinaga Foundation approved new grants for 2,196 students, or 63.7 percent of the applicants.

A total of 4,946 high school students are currently receiving Ashinaga scholarships.

The Ashinaga Foundation conducted a survey in August this year, covering 4,590 guardians of children receiving grants under the scholarship program. It received responses from 59.6 percent of them.

The survey found that 91.6 percent of respondents had reduced spending on food, while 15.7 percent acknowledged they had been unable to pay their rent at least once during the past year.

Respondents reported an average annual income of 1.781 million yen, little changed from 1.764 million yen in the comparable 2021 survey.

Asked about the impact of rising prices on education, 21.5 percent said they had already “given up on attending a university, college or vocational school, or feared they might have to.”

The Ashinaga Foundation plans to provide financial aid to more recipients by raising awareness of its program and strengthening fundraising efforts.

NEW AID FOR 6TH-GRADERS

The Ashinaga Foundation on Sept. 17 also announced plans to start a program offering one-time grants to sixth-grade elementary school students to help them prepare for junior high school.

The foundation will provide 50,000 yen each to 400 elementary school students to help cover rising costs for school uniforms and educational materials.

The Ashinaga Foundation hopes the one-off payment will serve as an entry point to ongoing support, including the provision of information on other assistance programs.

articles.originalTitle: SpaceX successfully catches Starship and makes history
articles.originalText: The company's spacecraft returned to its Texas launchpad in dramatic fashion — by carefully lowering itself until two metal arms attached to the launch tower could secure it.
articles.originalFullText:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday's liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.

Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.

The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster's messy miss.

"Can you believe it?" shouted SpaceX commentator Dan Huot.

SpaceX officials said Saturday's catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, intended for moon and Mars travel. Although Friday's booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA welcomed Saturday's news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk's ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.

The world's largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX's Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission's one to two laps.

It was SpaceX's 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.

SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

As for the booster, SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster's guidance system sensed it wasn't in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA's next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.

Artemis III's four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin's Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity's first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.
articles.fullText:
Звездолет SpaceX совершил триумфальное возвращение на Землю в субботу, пойманный в воздухе гигантскими механическими руками, где его путешествие началось 22 часами ранее.

Это был грандиозный финал, на который надеялись Илон Маск и его команда — первый в истории захват космического корабля. Но с первой ступенью ракеты-носителя, взорвавшейся вскоре после пятничного взлета из Техаса, компания не достигла желаемого двойного улова.

Обломки остались в Мексиканском заливе, оцепленные буями, так как космический корабль в форме пули из нержавеющей стали опустился прямо на стартовую площадку.

Драматический, научно-фантастический захват помог искоренить беспорядочную промах бустера.

«Ты можешь в это поверить?» — закричал комментатор SpaceX Дэн Хуот.

Представители SpaceX заявили, что субботний улов демонстрирует полное повторное использование Starship, предназначенного для путешествий на Луну и Марс. Хотя восстановление ускорителя в пятницу не удалось, компания уже сделала три предыдущих улова, проверив технику.

НАСА приветствует субботние новости. Космическое агентство платит миллиарды долларов за Starship, чтобы высадить астронавтов Артемиды на Луну в конце этого десятилетия и помочь построить постоянную лунную базу. Амбиции Маска еще более грандиозны: он хочет запустить флот Starships, чтобы построить город на Марсе.

Самая большая и мощная ракета в мире — 407-футовый (124-метровый) бегемот — взорвалась в пятницу днем с базы SpaceX Starship недалеко от границы США и Мексики. Отделившись аккуратно от своего ускорителя, прежде чем все пошло наперекосяк, космический корабль на верхней ступени взлетел на орбиту и выпустил 26 передовых спутников Starlink.

Звёздный корабль продолжал кружить вокруг света на 165 миль (265 километров) вверх, с живым видом на себя и Землю, струящуюся вниз через Starlink. Космический корабль совершил 14 кругов вокруг Земли, затмив один-два круга предыдущей миссии.

Это был 15-й полет SpaceX полномасштабного звездолета с 2023 года и его единственная вторая поездка на орбиту.

SpaceX сообщила, что все на космическом корабле, включая его жизненно важный тепловой экран, похоже, работает хорошо.

Что касается ракеты-носителя, Кейт Тайс из SpaceX заявила, что ее двигатели прекратили работать слишком рано на обратном пути. Система наведения бустера почувствовала, что он не в правильном положении, и автоматически инициировала водный объезд и самоуничтожение. Инженеры до сих пор изучают причину.

SpaceX планирует начать запуск Starships из Космического центра Кеннеди во Флориде в ближайшие несколько месяцев. Это отправная точка для следующей миссии NASA Artemis, которая пропустит Луну и останется на орбите вокруг Земли для практики лунных посадочных аппаратов.

Четыре астронавта Artemis III попытаются пристыковать свою капсулу не только со звездолетом, но и с голубой луной Blue Origin. Обе компании будут по очереди доставлять экипажи на лунную поверхность. НАСА планирует в 2028 году совершить первую посадку на Луну со времен Аполлона более полувека назад.

articles.originalTitle: Макрон пригрозил критикам помощи Украине «новой войной»
articles.originalFullText:
Президент Франции Эммануэль Макрон резко высказался о критиках помощи Украине, пригрозив им «новой войной». Об этом он написал на своей странице в соцсети Х.

«Те, кто хотят ограничить ресурсы Украины, в сущности, стремятся сделать ее уязвимой, а вместе с тем и всю Европу. Это дух поражения. Это рецепт для новой войны. Франция не может разделять такую позицию», — сказал он.

По его словам, у Европы сейчас есть два приоритета: помочь Украине «пережить зиму» и вместе с Киевом достичь «справедливого и прочного мира». Он отметил, что мир, который может быть достигнут в случае прекращения помощи Украине, будет «несправедливым».

Ранее Макрон призвал Европу определить свои приоритеты на период после завершения конфликта на Украине и донести их до России.

articles.originalTitle: Democrats push back on Duffy’s demand for $50 billion to upgrade air traffic systems.
articles.originalFullText:
Latest

Federal officials said the cascading communications failures that forced the government to shut down flights across the United States on Friday started with a contractor upgrading air traffic control equipment, replacing copper wire with fiber optic cable.

The upgrade set off communications failures across the facilities that manage the national air space, the officials said. Alarmed at the scope of the problem, the Federal Aviation Administration decided to issue a rare nationwide ground stop for several hours.

Speaking at news conference in Washington, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the specific problem with the upgrade, which took place in what he called a “remote” facility, was not yet known. The contractor, L3Harris, has worked for the Federal Aviation Administration for decades, he said.

Mr. Duffy said his agency was trying to determine whether the problem had been caused by the contractor’s incompetence or faulty equipment. “We haven’t determined what the fault was,” he said. He added, “We’re going to hold people accountable.”

The F.A.A. administrator, Bryan Bedford, said there was no evidence the communication problems had stemmed from a cyberattack or the use of artificial intelligence.

Mr. Bedford said that he expected the system to be back to normal by Sunday night. “The worst is behind us,” he said.

But even though the system came back online Friday evening, the effects of the shutdown were vast and continued on Saturday.

Travelers across the United States were still facing delays and cancellations on Saturday as airlines and airports struggled to recover from the ground stop.

At least 3,000 flights scheduled for Saturday were canceled, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm. At Chicago O’Hare International Airport, a ground stop was issued for United Airlines flights.

Mr. Duffy again called on lawmakers to fully fund upgrades that he said were needed to prevent similar failures. To upgrade aging air traffic facilities and technology, he said, he wanted another $50 billion from the Republican-controlled Congress, which last year approved $12.5 billion for the project.

Here’s what else to know:

If your flight is canceled: You are entitled to a refund if your flight is canceled in the United States, regardless of the reason, or if a flight is significantly delayed or changed and you decide not to take it. Here are other travel tips that might be helpful. Read more ›

Handling the chaos: Radio transmissions between air traffic controllers and pilots at major airports offered a peek at how they navigated the ground stop. Read more ›

Rare halt: Friday’s nationwide ground stop was only the third that the F.A.A. has issued this century. It ranks as the second-longest, after the stop issued in the wake of the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001. There was a shorter one on Jan. 11, 2023, because of an outage in the F.A.A.’s safety-alert system. Read more ›

Democrats’ response: Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the House’s top-ranking Democrat, said the stop was “the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents” under the Trump administration. He added that Americans deserved timely answers about how and why it happened.

With flights grounded for nearly five hours Friday evening, Americans heard from the homeland security secretary. They heard from the transportation secretary. They did not hear from President Trump.

At least not about the nationwide ground stop, the first major crisis the federal government has faced since the midterm elections. The halt grounded or delayed some 10,000 flights from coast to coast and confirmed what experts have been warning for years: that the nation’s flight safety system is perilously fragile.

Instead, the president, who remained behind the scenes at the White House, posted messages to social media that night on other topics.

“MAKE OUR ENTERTAINMENT INDUSTRY GREAT AGAIN!” he wrote on Truth Social, in the middle of the crisis, calling for tax incentives to lure movie production back to the United States.

The absence of Mr. Trump, who has made few public appearances since Democrats swept the midterms, seemed notable enough that Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, sought to assure the nation in the heat of the crisis on Friday night that the president was fully engaged, if not in his more common spot in front of the cameras.

“This is what President Trump does,” Mr. Mullin said in a news conference. “He puts leaders in place, and he allows them to lead. They even ask, you know, why is the president not talking? It’s because he’s allowed Secretary Duffy and us to go out there and explain to you what took place.” He was referring to Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, who appeared beside Mr. Mullin on Friday night.

By Saturday morning, Mr. Trump still hadn’t commented on the ground stop. Instead, he began attacking Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, a Democrat and political rival, over his commutation of death penalty sentences for more than 500 inmates, an action the governor took more than a week ago.

It is an old strategy in politics to let underlings be the bearers of bad news. Mr. Trump’s decision not to engage in public on a crisis with cascading effects across the country comes as Democrats in Congress have already vowed to investigate the administration’s handling of the shutdown.

With Mr. Trump steering clear of the topic on Friday night, Mr. Mullin and Mr. Duffy appeared at times to contradict each other as they tried to explain the breakdown that affected tens of thousands of people.

Transportation Department officials, in particular, were caught off guard when Mr. Mullin told reporters that the meltdown had occurred because new technology upgrades had “overwhelmed the older system,” according to two people familiar with the matter.

At the time, department officials had not made a determination of what precisely had overloaded the antiquated system and caused the meltdown to spiral across the country. Mr. Duffy also tried to gently redirect after Mr. Mullin’s remarks, stressing that old equipment, not new technology, was what had overloaded and failed. On Saturday, Mr. Duffy told reporters that a routine router replacement in a remote area had triggered the nationwide outages but officials could not yet say whether it had been because of a faulty part or a contractor error.

In a statement on Saturday, Mr. Duffy said: “We’re deeply grateful for Secretary Mullin and his team’s partnership as we worked through this challenging time.”

When asked where Mr. Trump was during the ground stop, the officials defended the president and heaped praise on him.

“Well, the two of us have talked to him,” Mr. Duffy said. “He’s in. I’ve talked to him on the phone. I’ve talked to him in the Oval. So has Markwayne.”

As the agency leaders addressed the media, Stephen Miller, the newly installed White House chief of staff, and Steven Cheung, the communications director, watched off to the side.

Asked for comment, the White House referred to the comments of Mr. Duffy and Mr. Mullin.

Mr. Duffy said Congress was to blame for the ground stop because the legislative branch had failed to fund updated technology for the Federal Aviation Administration. Lawmakers have privately questioned how efficiently the F.A.A. has spent money already appropriated, congressional aides say, and Democrats say the administration has prioritized issues like deportations over air safety.

“I want $50 billion,” Mr. Duffy said. “President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people.”

He added: “And when Secretary Duffy said he’s the greatest president we’ve had. You’ve never had a builder and a leader like President Trump lead this nation, have a vision and put the team together.”

Ever since Republicans were routed in the midterm elections, Mr. Trump has been keeping somewhat of a lower profile. Before the midterms, he embarked on a blitz of rallies across the country in which he spoke to the public nearly every night.

This week, he appeared in public sparingly: once at an impromptu appearance with the U.F.C. president Dana White as a follow-up to a post that Mr. Trump acknowledged was an attempt to distract from bad news cycles, and at a speech on Veterans Day.

Former Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene, Republican of Georgia, who was once a close ally of the president’s, noted that Mr. Trump has never been shy in putting his full focus on his construction projects, such as the attempted repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. But she noted that he seemed unengaged during the F.A.A. crisis.

“Trump constantly railed about fixing the reflection pool so much that he used the last day before massively losing the midterms to give a speech in front of the reflection pool bragging about he fixed the reflection pool,” she wrote on social media. But in a crisis that led to Mr. Duffy’s call for billions to upgrade air traffic systems, she wrote, “President Trump doesn’t even issue so much as a Truth Social post.”

She added: “While everyone was freaking out thinking we are under some sort of attack, Trump didn’t even bother to address the nation.”

On Saturday afternoon, Mr. Trump finally publicly acknowledged the matter, but only obliquely and through another’s words. He posted a quote attributed to Senator John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana, that appeared to reference a desire for more funding for the F.A.A.: “The FAA Funding should be a stand alone Bill — We should get Democrat support for that!”

With the crisis largely over, though with many flights still canceled and disruption rife, the president posted again about the need for tax credits for the movie industry.

Maggie Haberman, Karoun Demirjian and Kate Kelly contributed reporting.

The hourslong halt to departing flights across the country on Friday started with routine maintenance on air traffic control equipment at a remote site, federal officials said on Saturday.

That work was being carried out by L3Harris Technologies, a little-known defense contractor that owns and operates essential communications infrastructure used by the Federal Aviation Administration.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stopped short of saying that the company was at fault, but he vowed to investigate whether it bears responsibility.

“What did L3Harris do? Did they make mistakes yesterday?” he said at a news conference on Saturday. “They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it. Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. And frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”

In a statement on Saturday, L3Harris said that it was supporting the F.A.A. investigation into what had happened and that it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

The company was formed in 2019, the result of a merger of two defense contractors. It employed about 45,000 people at the start of this year and is based in Florida.

About 75 percent of its revenue comes from U.S. government contracts, many of them for the military. In 2025, the company was selected to retrofit a Boeing 747 donated by Qatar to be used as the interim Air Force One. L3Harris has generated more than $1 billion in annual profits since 2020.

The company also does a lot of work for the F.A.A., including maintaining networks that facilitate communications between air traffic controllers and pilots and receive plane location signals.

L3Harris owns the equipment used to transmit voice communications and data to and from air traffic control facilities, remote radar sites and weather stations, a network known as the F.A.A. Telecommunications Infrastructure. The company is in the midst of upgrading the copper wires used in that network to high-speed fiber optic cable across more than 4,400 sites, with over 70 percent of those lines already replaced.

Federal officials said on Saturday that they had halted departing flights a day earlier because of a communications disruption set off by a copper-to-fiber upgrade at a remote site, which they did not identify. A newly installed router began firing more than a thousand connection requests every few seconds, which disrupted voice communications and radar feeds. Ultimately, it took technicians 45 minutes to identify the problem.

The F.A.A. is trying to build a modern replacement to its telecommunications network with other partners, including AT&T and Verizon, over the next few years, Secretary Duffy said on Saturday. “Until I can build that, I’m stuck with L3Harris,” he said.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, on Friday requested $50 billion for a “complete overhaul” of the aging air traffic control system, laying much of the blame on Congress after flights across the nation were halted for hours.

Mr. Duffy’s demand thrust the funding issue to the forefront of the final days of Republican control on Capitol Hill.

Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News on Saturday morning that he would seek to add more funding for the Federal Aviation Administration into an “aggressive legislative package” he planned to put forth in the lame-duck session of Congress.

Democrats said the Trump administration had plenty of money it could put toward improving an outdated air traffic control system — funds it was using instead for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. They said Congress needed to begin investigating the failures of the Trump administration.

Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion to help pay for upgrades to the air traffic communications system. Republican lawmakers have introduced the Modern Skies Act in the House and Senate, a bill that would authorize another $30 billion in upgrades.

That bill seeks to allocate $10.1 billon for air traffic control modernization, $10 billion for control towers and airport improvements, and another $10 billion for an aging terminal pilot program.

But the bill has no Democratic co-sponsors. And on Friday night, Democrats said the airport crisis was caused by how the Trump administration had allocated money and overseen the F.A.A.

Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, said that Mr. Duffy’s request for another $50 billion was alarming, given that Republicans had “showered ICE with billions in funding.”

He added that “if this administration is serious about aviation safety, it should stop making excuses and work with Congress to put taxpayer dollars where they’re actually needed.”

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, blamed the breakdown on the Trump administration.

“From Day 1, instead of taking responsibility, MAGA extremists have fired and scapegoated hard-working federal employees whose job it is to keep our skies safe, particularly women and people of color,” he said.

House Democrats promised an investigation next year into how air traffic was brought to a standstill. “Preserve all documents and emails,” Democrats on the committee overseeing homeland security and the Transportation Security Administration wrote online. “Oversight is coming.”

Senator Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, the senior Democrat on the subcommittee overseeing aviation, demanded a thorough investigation into the F.A.A.

Mr. Johnson, however, said that “we don’t really need any investigation to understand we need further investment.”

At a news conference on Friday night, Mr. Duffy said the issues were not partisan.

“It’s not Democrat, it’s not Republican. It’s American,” he said. “Give us the money to fix it.”

At the Detroit airport — long one of my favorites because of the bright red tram and, more recently, a chance run-in with ex-N.B.A. star Jalen Rose — travelers have packed the food courts and bars as they wait for flights, delayed or otherwise.

The televisions next to the airport outpost of Buddy’s, which lays claim to inventing Detroit-style pizza, are playing the Saturday afternoon slate of college football games, including, of course, the University of Michigan’s matchup with Oregon.

On Saturday afternoon, San Francisco International Airport still showed the effects of a ground stop called by the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday. Crowds were moderate, travelers were sleeping in gates and hallways of the airport and the screens showed many delays and cancellations.

Thousands of passengers scrambled to update their travel plans on Saturday as air traffic slowly unsnarled after a nationwide ground stop on Friday, but a number of travelers had already arrived at their destinations on flights left unaffected by the order.

Dozens of international flights took to the skies even as airports across the United States coped with only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration this century. Certain flights were also permitted to depart from the West Coast to Hawaii during the stoppage.

Here’s why some air travel was allowed to proceed even as flight systems were hampered.

Some international flights were able to depart.

More than 8,200 flights were canceled nationwide on Friday — over 31 percent of those scheduled — according to Cirium, an aviation data firm.

But more than 60 flights bound for overseas left the United States during the stoppage, according to Flightradar24, an aviation tracking site.

There are 21 air traffic control facilities, 20 in the contiguous United States and one in Alaska, that oversee swaths of regions throughout the country, according to the F.A.A.

As some of those centers recovered, flights were “allowed to depart through coordination with the Air Traffic Control System Command Center,” the F.A.A. said in an advisory less than two hours after the ground stop was ordered.

Flights departing for Europe from the Midwest or the East Coast can communicate with the Canadian authorities, said Dan Bubb, a former commercial pilot and an aviation history professor at the University of Las Vegas, Nevada.

Additionally, air traffic over the open ocean is less congested compared with that of the contiguous United States, he said.

Nick Daniels, the president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, said that for planes traveling such a large distance over oceanic airspace, “they have process procedures, different standards of separations, than what we do to run the volume of air traffic” in the lower 48 states.

What about domestic flights to Hawaii or Alaska?

At 3 p.m. Pacific Standard Time on Friday, about two hours before the nationwide ground stop was lifted, San Francisco International Airport said that Pacific-bound flights, including to Hawaii and Asia, had been cleared for departure.

Why were passengers flying west so fortunate?

Those pilots generally will talk to one of the regional centers until reaching cruising altitude, Dr. Bubb said.

Centers handling air traffic headed to Hawaii or Asia are outside the contiguous United States, and therefore could avoid long delays from the ground stop, he said. At a certain altitude, a pilot could swap communications with California controllers for those in Hawaii or Alaska, he added.

Flights within Alaska, those from the West Coast to Hawaii and international flights from Honolulu were also exempt from the ground stop, Alaska Airlines said in statement.

Areas like Alaska, Guam and Hawaii are far enough removed that they can remain stable even as systems are affected in the contiguous United States, Mr. Daniels said.

“If they would have seen any kind of risk in the system there as well, then they would have reacted the same to reduce the capacity,” he added.

Can medical aircraft fly during a ground stop?

Generally, yes.

During ground stops and delays, emergency and medical aircraft are given clearance to take off.

Life Flight Network, a medical transport service, said in a social media post on Friday that “EMS aircraft are exempt from this restriction,” and its services were operating normally.

“Above all is medevac and law enforcement,” Mr. Daniels said. “They get a priority movement throughout the system, and we move other aircraft out of their way, versus, they need to get in line with everyone else.”

Communications continued despite the stoppage.

Pilots and controllers have many tools to communicate, Dr. Bubb said.

Pilots can talk to one another, their companies and ground control through different messaging systems even if one fails.

“There are redundant systems where pilots can talk to each other, and we can sequence ourselves, but we follow the instructions that we were given by air traffic control,” Dr. Bubb said.

At about 11 a.m. inside the Tom Bradley international terminal at Los Angeles International Airport, the check-in area flight boards showed no delays and things appeared to be moving smoothly.

L3Harris, the federal contractor that was updating air traffic control equipment prior to the nationwide outage, said in a statement that they took the nationwide ground stop seriously. The contractor said it had completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. The company added it was supporting the F.A.A. in its investigation.

The National Football League said this weekend’s games would go forward as planned, but that the league had “adjusted its officiating assignments” by “reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns,” Brian McCarthy, a spokesman, wrote in an email.

As the effects of Friday’s ground stop continue to ripple outward, Princess Cruises said it would delay departure times for three ships set to leave from U.S. ports on Saturday to allow passengers extra time to account for travel delays. The postponed sail times would not affect cruise itineraries, a spokesperson wrote in an email.

Travelers across the United States on Saturday morning were still feeling the frustrating, plan-ruining aftershocks of the ground stop that halted air travel for hours on Friday.

“I’ve been right here for 20 hours,” said Jasmine Harp, a passenger at Kennedy International Airport in New York. “I have not showered, I have not slept. It’s torture.”

Ms. Harp, 25, was going on 48 hours of travel, trying to get home to Detroit after spending a week in Paris for her birthday.

She had just sat down in her airplane seat on Friday when the pilot told passengers to deplane. A few hours later, the flight was canceled. She described a mad dash to the baggage claim, where passengers worked to secure their luggage.

“They just dumped everybody’s bags off all at once,” she said. “It was chaotic.”

To make matters worse, Ms. Harp had left the gate area but still had to wait for her rebooked flight, which was to depart at 3 p.m. the next day. That meant no restaurants, no shops and, most uncomfortably, no seats. She found a luggage counter to perch on.

“I wish they would let me in the lounge,” she said Saturday morning, as she broke out some trail mix that she had rationed throughout the night.

Antonio Alemán, 39, whose transfer to Lima, Peru, was canceled late on Friday, spent an uncomfortable night at the same airport. The airline, Latam, rebooked him on a flight for Tuesday. “I don’t know where I will stay until then,” he said.

Further south, the scene at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport looked, at first glance, as if it might have been a typical Saturday morning, with passengers checking bags and waiting at security checkpoints.

A closer inspection, however, revealed travelers sleeping in the airport’s quiet corners, departure screens speckled with cancellation and delay notices, and backups at customer service desks.

Barefoot and sprawled out on the carpeted floor in Hartsfield-Jackson’s central atrium, Glory Agunbiade, 16, and her mother, Itanola Agunbiade, 56, had managed to steal four or five hours of sleep after their Friday flight to Indianapolis was canceled.

From their makeshift campsite — they each used their bags as pillows — the pair bickered over how the federal government had handled Friday’s ground stop. While the elder Ms. Agunbiade saw the decision to halt flights as a necessary precaution and said it was “not anybody’s fault,” her teenage daughter was more frustrated.

“It’s like all we know is that the problem was about communication,” the younger Ms. Agunbiade said. “I feel like we’re entitled to more information.”

In Chicago, Pedro and Aorbys Vasquez were resting at O’Hare International Airport on Saturday, more than 12 hours after their connecting flight to Paris was supposed to leave. Their original flight was delayed six times before it was finally canceled. By that point, they could not find an available hotel room.

The couple slept in seats with nothing more than neck pillows to comfort them. Their new flight is scheduled for 6:45 p.m., 24 hours after they were originally scheduled to depart.

Looking at the bright side of an experience he called exhausting, Vasquez joked, “at least we shouldn’t have a problem sleeping on our flight.”

Robert Chiarito and Sean Keenan contributed reporting.

Randy Near, 58, a home inspector from Washington State, was furious on Saturday as he waited with a pile of luggage, while his 24-year-old son Charlie stood in the line at Terminal 3 at Los Angeles International Airport with dozens of people, hoping to get them on the next flight home to Seattle. He hadn’t slept in 36 hours.

“Look, our entire infrastructure, from the highway system to the F.A.A., is a joke,” he said. “You go to any other Western country, and they have Wi-Fi, fiber optics, good freeways, good bridges, and we are here living in the freaking dark ages and being force-fed this lie that we are somehow the greatest country in the world.”

“Both parties pay a lot of lip service to bills that support infrastructure in this country, and as soon as soon as they get elected, that sort of stuff gets forgotten,” he added.

The communications failures that prompted Federal Aviation Administration officials to issue a nationwide ground stop started when L3 Harris, a contractor managing the agency’s telecoms network, made a standard upgrade at a remote air traffic location, federal officials said Saturday.

The contractor was conducting work on Friday that was needed to replace aging analog copper wire with more modern fiber optic cable, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, told reporters. The “routine” task was being done at a location remote and small enough that officials assumed a Friday afternoon upgrade would pose no meaningful disruption to the air traffic, he said.

That presumption proved wrong, as the changeover from copper to fiber started flooding the system with levels of data it could not handle, triggering a cascade of communications failures across the air traffic facilities that manage the national air space. Officials, alarmed at the scope of the problems, decided to issue a rare nationwide ground stop for hours.

As of Saturday morning, administration officials still have not determined whether L3 Harris or shoddy equipment was at fault.

“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning it was user error or installer error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router?” Mr. Duffy told reporters. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”

Representatives for L3 Harris did not immediately return email and phone requests for comment on Saturday.

L3 Harris has been managing the F.A.A.’s effort to shift its antiquated communications system of analog copper lines to a nationwide network of fiber optic cable. Earlier this month, the company boasted that they had completed such upgrades at 70 percent of air traffic control facilities, a figure that F.A.A. administrator Bryan Bedford echoed at Saturday’s news conference.

Such upgrades — which Mr. Bedford characterized as “sustainment,” not modernization — are vital to ensure that the air traffic control system can operate safely, he and Mr. Duffy told reporters.

Officials were sure, Mr. Duffy said, that they had identified the origin of the problem; for instance, when they isolated the location and took it offline, the system’s functionality was restored. There was no evidence that nefarious activity, or the agency’s recent efforts to outfit its air traffic control facilities with assistive A.I. technology, had played a role in triggering Friday’s problems, he and Mr. Bedford added.

But the episode raises serious questions about how well the F.A.A. understands the potential vulnerabilities of their existing network as it makes patches and upgrades to antiquated technology.

The routers in air traffic control facilities, which became overloaded with over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, were mostly manufactured in 2001, Mr. Duffy said, and were out of service by 2006.

“Was it a faulty installation? Was it a faulty configuration? Or was it just a bad piece of faulty technology?” Mr. Bedford said, without offering a conclusion.

He added that officials would have to reassess their protocols, and “pivot” in the future to avoid causing similar sweeping problems when upgrading equipment.

Traffic at Los Angeles International Airport was robust on Saturday, with travelers being dropped off curbside. Airplanes appeared to be taking off and landing at a slower pace than on a normal day. Inside Terminal 3, Delta check-in counters were jammed with travelers dropping off bags. The departures and arrivals screens showed several canceled flights, but a majority of flights were listed as boarding, at the gate or on time.

The near-total shutdown of the nation’s airspace ended on Friday evening, but its ripple effects continued into Saturday as airlines canceled thousands of flights.

By Saturday morning, almost 15 percent of the day’s flights had been scrapped, and the number was still climbing. The recovery will most likely last for days as airlines work to juggle their schedules, rebook passengers and reposition planes.

Aviation functions like a relay race. To work well, many things have to align in the same place at the same time, including the availability of planes, crews and an open airport gate.

On Friday, thousands of planes were pulled from the air, filling up limited space on the ground. Many returned to the airports they had just left, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm. Jets at crowded airports weren’t allowed to depart and sat idle while flight crews quickly hit their legal working limits.

Pilots are generally limited to eight or nine hours of flying and a total shift length of 9 to 14 hours, though union contracts and airline policies often shrink those windows. Flight attendants are also governed by limits on the length of their shift. Both must receive lengthy breaks in between shifts, too.

For instance, a pilot who was scheduled to fly from New York to Miami on Friday night could easily have timed out while waiting for the ground stop to end. That would have left the airline struggling to find replacement pilots not only for the flight from New York, but also for the flight that pilot was scheduled to operate out of Miami on Saturday. Multiply that by hundreds and airline schedules can quickly implode.

Take N865DN, the tail number for a Boeing 737 operated by Delta Air Lines. It started Friday flying from Charleston, S.C., to Atlanta. From there, it made round trip flights to Louisville, Ky., and Norfolk, Va., returning to Atlanta, according to Flightradar24, a flight-tracking service.

The plane was supposed to fly on to Savannah, Ga., back to Atlanta, and then to Chicago, where it would start the day on Saturday. But it never made those last three flights.

Delta rebuilt its Saturday plan, with the plane scheduled to fly from Atlanta to Spokane, Wash., and on to Salt Lake City and Raleigh-Durham, N.C.

For minor disruptions, airlines can play catch-up by restarting flights and trying to make up for lost time. But bigger disruptions, such as the one that occurred Friday, often require resetting the network by proactively canceling many flights.

At long last, the line to pick up luggage checked for Friday flights is shrinking, baggage claim carousels are whirling, and departure screens are becoming slightly less colorful. The Atlanta airport is starting to look like its old self.

The balcony in Hartsfield-Jackson’s central atrium remains a sort of campsite for weary travelers whose flights have been delayed or canceled. Some bought neck pillows and blankets downstairs. Others claimed the airport’s complimentary wheelchairs. Most slept on their luggage.

The security line at O’Hare’s Terminal One, from which United Airlines operates, was virtually nonexistent Saturday at 10:50 a.m. local time. Possibly because most United Airlines flights appear to be delayed or canceled.

The F.A.A. has not extended a ground stop for United Airlines flights at Chicago O’Hare International Airport, which was scheduled to end at 11 a.m. Eastern, according to an agency alert. About 13 percent of the 616 United flights scheduled to depart from the airport have been canceled as of 11:20 a.m., according to Cirium, an aviation data firm. United is headquartered in Chicago.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, repeatedly stressed throughout his news conference that he would choose safety over inconvenience, acknowledging that passengers will miss weddings, birthday parties and work trips this weekend.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, has now twice mentioned that college football games have been disrupted by the fight cancellations and delays caused by Friday’s ground stop.

Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administator, said no air traffic facilities went entirely dark, but the F.A.A. received reports of certain frequencies going in and out. The issue popped up in more than 10 facilities. That’s when the F.A.A. realized something larger was going on and ordered a national ground stop.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said his agency was able to isolate the location where the faulty upgrade work was done and take it offline. “We feel very comfortable that was the root cause,” Duffy said. “It wasn’t a foreign actor.” He said what happened Friday raised questions for the contractor, L3 Harris, about what went wrong. “We’re going to hold people accountable,” he said.

The ground stop that brought air travel across the country to a halt Friday evening highlighted persistent weaknesses in the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure, which has had several disruptive failures in recent months.

Two months ago, a circuit failure and severed fiber optic cable caused crippling ground stops and delays at airports along the East Coast. Smaller outages unfolded in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina and George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston, when contractors accidentally cut into fiber line.

The Friday ground stop, which was only the third the F.A.A. has issued this century, eclipsed the fallout of previous air traffic communications equipment failures. Officials said it was prompted by efforts to replace an outdated router, which caused circuits in the national air traffic network to become overloaded and fail, interrupting communication lines between air traffic controllers and pilots.

By Saturday, thousands of flights had been canceled, and airports were still crowded with stranded travelers. The recovery will most likely take days, as airlines rebook passengers and reposition planes.

Friday’s breakdown, and the earlier episodes, have underscored the structural vulnerabilities that hamper controllers’ ability to safely manage flight traffic, even after improvements. And they have raised questions about whether federal authorities have done enough to create backup systems to prevent disruptive or catastrophic failures.

Friday’s incident touched off a blame game in Washington. Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, accused Congress of failing to pony up for systemwide upgrades.

“How many more times does this have to happen for Congress to give the money to fix it?” he asked reporters at the White House.

He demanded that lawmakers approve $50 billion in emergency funds for the project, tens of billions more than he had previously requested. He did not explain how the money would be spent, but said that his department had been forced to pursue insufficient patchwork upgrades.

Last year, Congress gave the F.A.A. $12.5 billion to fuel its air traffic modernization plan. But according to a September report from the Government Accountability Office, the F.A.A. was juggling 11,389 modernization projects that had not been integrated, predicting that a lack of better coordination would “increase the likelihood of F.A.A. repeating its history of cost overruns, delays and unmet performance targets.”

Congressional aides say that lawmakers in both parties have also expressed skepticism about Mr. Duffy’s use of the appropriated money, including whether it is being spent efficiently.

For decades, air traffic communications have relied on a system that runs on analog copper wire, floppy disks and alphabetical keyboards so old that the F.A.A. has difficulty sourcing spare parts. Congress approved its first tranche of modernization funds after faulty equipment caused a series of outages in traffic control facilities, including the one serving Newark Liberty International Airport, leading to alarming losses of radar and other communications capabilities.

Earlier this month, L3 Harris, the primary telecommunications contractor tasked with managing the system upgrades, said on its website that it had converted about 70 percent of the copper line to fiber optic cable. And last week, the F.A.A. announced it would begin to phase out floppy disks.

In a statement, L3 Harris said that it was supporting the F.A.A. in its investigation of what led to Friday’s meltdown, and that it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

The disruptions in recent weeks have also revealed that even the upgrades the F.A.A. has made have sometimes had serious vulnerabilities.

In September, when a circuit at a regional air traffic facility failed, operators had no backup options beyond the fiber line, 600 feet of which they discovered had been severed by a construction crew in New Jersey working on an Amtrak project. More than 430 flights were canceled before the system was fixed several hours later.

A similar incident occurred in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport, when a plumbing contractor accidentally severed a fiber line. The airport was forced to issue a ground stop for several hours. A day later, officials were forced to issue a ground stop at George Bush Intercontinental Airport, when another contractor inadvertently severed a fiber line.

Bryan Bedford, the F.A.A. administrator, told reporters at the time that the fiber line upgrades were not enough to save the system from failure. And the F.A.A. had yet to incorporate the sort of cloud services that could provide additional redundancies.

“There’s no backup to the backup,” he told reporters at a Saturday news conference.

Since last year, Mr. Duffy’s requests for air traffic funding have crept up. After Congress approved $12.5 billion in air traffic modernization last year — $7.75 billion of which was dedicated to telecommunications and radar upgrades — Mr. Duffy said publicly that he would need another $19 to $20 billion to complete the work.
